question: When does a merge conflict occur in Git?
options: When two branches change the same lines of the same file differently
Whenever any two branches are merged
When a branch has no commits
When the remote server is offline
explanation: A conflict arises when Git cannot automatically reconcile changes because both branches modified the same region of a file.

question: In a conflicted file, what does the marker '<<<<<<<' indicate?
options: The end of the file
The start of the changes from your current branch (HEAD)
A comment to be ignored
The location of the remote server
explanation: The <<<<<<< marker begins the section containing your current branch's version, followed by ======= and then the incoming branch's version.

question: After manually editing files to resolve a conflict, what must you do to complete the merge?
options: Run git reset --hard
Delete the .git folder
Do nothing; Git resolves it automatically
Run git add on the resolved files, then git commit
explanation: You stage the resolved files with git add to mark the conflict resolved, then commit to finalize the merge.

question: Which command aborts an in-progress merge and returns to the pre-merge state?
options: git merge --abort
git merge --cancel
git undo merge
git reset --soft
explanation: git merge --abort cancels the current merge attempt and restores the branch to its state before the merge began.

question: Which practice helps reduce the frequency and size of merge conflicts?
options: Never using branches at all
Committing only once a month
Pulling/rebasing frequently and keeping branches short-lived and focused
Editing every file in every commit
explanation: Integrating changes often and keeping feature branches small and short-lived limits divergence, reducing conflict likelihood and complexity.
